record.description: Cumulative energy transferred from a plasma-facing component into its coolant over the pulse, excluding energy retained in the component or transferred elsewhere.
record.documentation:
The quantity is the energy cumulatively absorbed by active coolant from a specified plasma-facing component during the accumulation interval. It represents thermal energy removed from that component, not an instantaneous transfer rate or the component's total deposited energy.

$$
E_{\mathrm{cool}}(t) = \int_{t_0}^{t} P_{\mathrm{cool}}(\tau)\,d\tau
$$

Here, $E_{\mathrm{cool}}(t)$ is the accumulated coolant-absorbed energy at evaluation time $t$; $t_0$ is the pulse start and lower limit of accumulation; $P_{\mathrm{cool}}(\tau)$ is the instantaneous thermal power extracted by the coolant from the component at integration time $\tau$. The power corresponds to the wall coolant-removal concept described by [total thermal coolant-absorbed power at the wall](name:total_thermal_coolant_absorbed_power_at_wall).

The scope is one specified plasma-facing component and its active coolant, with contributions accumulated from pulse start to the evaluation time. Only energy transferred into that coolant is included; energy retained in the component, radiated away, carried by particles, or transferred to unrelated coolant circuits is excluded.

The accumulated energy is the time integral of the corresponding coolant-absorbed power, so its time derivative equals $P_{\mathrm{cool}}(t)$ when the accumulation is continuous. It is therefore distinct from the instantaneous power quantity and from deposited energy that has not necessarily been removed by coolant.

record.description: Normalized count at detector pixel is the detector-pixel count divided by a positive count-equivalent reference from the same acquisition frame. It also covers count rates when numerator and reference use identical exposure normalization.
record.documentation:
Normalized count at detector pixel is the detector-pixel count divided by a positive count-equivalent reference from the same acquisition frame. The reference is a relative scale for that frame and must be common to the detector pixels whose normalized values are compared.

The defining ratio for detector pixel $p$ is

$$
C_\mathrm{norm}(p) = \frac{C(p)}{C_\mathrm{ref}}, \qquad C_\mathrm{ref} > 0
$$

where $C_\mathrm{norm}(p)$ is the normalized count, $C(p)$ is the [count at detector pixel], and $C_\mathrm{ref}$ is the positive count-equivalent reference for the same acquisition frame.

The same definition applies to count rates or exposure-normalized count-equivalent signals only when $C(p)$ and $C_\mathrm{ref}$ use identical time or exposure normalization. The quantity is a relative normalization; it does not specify whether $C_\mathrm{ref}$ is a total-frame, peak, mean, or externally specified reference count, and it is distinct from an absolute calibration factor.

record.description: Electrostatic potential at wall is the voltage-valued scalar potential of the plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing wall, relative to a chosen electrical reference.
record.documentation:
Electrostatic potential at wall is the voltage-valued scalar potential of the plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing wall, relative to a chosen electrical reference. It is the wall-local restriction of [electrostatic potential](name:electrostatic_potential).

The electrostatic contribution to the electric field is defined by

$$
\mathbf{E}_{\rm es} = -\nabla \Phi
$$

where $\Phi$ is the electrostatic potential, $\mathbf{E}_{\rm es}$ is the electrostatic electric field, and $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient.

This quantity refers to the plasma-side potential adjacent to the wall, not the electrical potential of the wall material, an applied wall bias, or the [floating electrostatic potential](name:floating_electrostatic_potential), which is established by a zero-net-current condition. The full electric field may additionally contain an inductive contribution.

Sign convention: Positive when a positive test charge has greater electrostatic potential energy at the specified location than at the chosen electrical reference.

record.description: Flux-surface average of the signed electric-field projection along the magnetic field, taken over the separatrix rather than at a single point.
record.documentation:
The flux-surface-averaged parallel electric field is the signed average of the electric-field projection along the local magnetic-field direction over the separatrix magnetic surface.

The defining flux-surface average is

$$
\left\langle E_\parallel \right\rangle_{\rm sep} = \frac{\displaystyle\oint_{\mathcal{C}_{\rm sep}} E_\parallel\,\frac{d\ell}{B}}{\displaystyle\oint_{\mathcal{C}_{\rm sep}}\frac{d\ell}{B}}
$$

where $\langle E_\parallel \rangle_{\rm sep}$ is the averaged quantity, $E_\parallel$ is the local projection of the electric field along the local magnetic field, $\mathcal{C}_{\rm sep}$ is the poloidal contour of the separatrix, $d\ell$ is the differential poloidal arc length, and $B$ is the magnitude of the local magnetic field. The subscript $\rm sep$ identifies the separatrix surface.

The quantity applies to the complete separatrix surface and uses the inverse-magnetic-field weighting intrinsic to a flux-surface average; it is not a pointwise value. It is the averaged counterpart of the local [parallel electric field at the separatrix](name:parallel_electric_field_at_separatrix), so local variation around the separatrix is combined rather than retained as a separate spatial value.

Sign convention: Positive when the electric field points along the local magnetic-field direction.

record.description: Volume-integrated rate of neutron production from fusion reactions in the plasma, summed over all neutron-producing reaction channels and all reacting-population classes, including thermonuclear, beam-thermal, and beam-beam contributions.
record.documentation:
Volume-integrated rate of neutron production from fusion reactions in the plasma, summed over all neutron-producing fusion reaction channels and all reacting-population classes: thermonuclear (thermal-thermal), beam-thermal, and beam-beam reactions. Neutrons born in non-fusion processes, such as photoneutron production or material activation, are excluded.

The defining aggregation is

$$
\Gamma_n^{\mathrm{fusion}} = \int_{V} S_n^{\mathrm{fusion}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV = \sum_{\alpha} \Gamma_{n,\alpha}
$$

where $\Gamma_n^{\mathrm{fusion}}$ is this quantity, $S_n^{\mathrm{fusion}}$ is the local neutron production rate density summed over all fusion channels, $V$ is the plasma volume, $\alpha$ runs over the neutron-producing reaction-channel and reacting-population classes, and $\Gamma_{n,\alpha}$ is the class-resolved volume-integrated production rate; the thermonuclear contribution to the integrand is the local [fusion neutron emissivity].

Each class-resolved summand $\Gamma_{n,\alpha}$ corresponds to a [neutron flux] scoped to a specified fusion-reaction class; this quantity is the sum of those class-resolved rates. The thermonuclear summand alone is the [total neutron source rate due to thermal fusion](name:total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion), and channel- and population-resolved members such as the [deuterium-tritium beam-beam neutron production rate] are components of the sum, not additional totals. Despite the word flux in the name, this quantity is a global source strength (a count rate), not a particle flux crossing a surface.

record.description: Root-mean-square wavelength spread of a spectrometer channel’s response about its reference vacuum wavelength, representing instrumental broadening for monochromatic input.
record.documentation:
The root-mean-square spectral width is the wavelength spread of a spectrometer channel’s instrumental response about its reference vacuum wavelength. It characterizes broadening produced by the channel rather than the intrinsic width of the incident spectral line.

For a monochromatic input, the width is the second-moment spread of the channel response:

$$
w_{\lambda,\mathrm{rms}} = \left[\frac{\int (\lambda-\lambda_0)^2 R(\lambda)\,d\lambda}{\int R(\lambda)\,d\lambda}\right]^{1/2}
$$

where $w_{\lambda,\mathrm{rms}}$ is the root-mean-square spectral width, $\lambda$ is vacuum wavelength, $\lambda_0$ is the channel reference vacuum wavelength, and $R(\lambda)$ is the channel spectral response.

This quantity applies to one spectrometer channel and aggregates the complete spectral response over wavelength through its second moment. It excludes physical broadening of the incident spectral line and is not an interval obtained by integrating the response.

The RMS width is the statistical form of [spectral width of a spectrometer channel](name:root_mean_square_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel); for a Gaussian response, it is the Gaussian standard deviation used by that parent quantity. It is distinct from the [effective spectral width of a spectrometer channel](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel), which is a response-equivalent wavelength interval rather than an RMS spread.

record.description: Toroidal normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam is the signed toroidal direction cosine k_phi/|k| of the electromagnetic wave vector at the beam launch point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
record.documentation:
Toroidal normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam is the signed toroidal direction cosine of the electromagnetic wave vector at the beam launch point. It is the projection of the local unit wave vector onto the toroidal basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The normalized toroidal component is defined by

$$
k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}} = \frac{\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\phi}}{\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert} = \frac{k_\phi}{\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert}
$$

where $\mathbf{k}$ is the electromagnetic wave vector at the beam launch point, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis with $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$, $k_\phi=\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is the [toroidal wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), and $\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert$ is the wave-vector magnitude.

This is a launch-point quantity, not an integral or average over a beam path. It is distinct from the [normalized toroidal wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:normalized_toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), which denotes the same toroidal direction cosine evaluated along a traced beam rather than specifically at launch. For real nonzero $\mathbf{k}$ it satisfies $-1 \leq k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}} \leq 1$; together with the [radial normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:radial_wave_vector_normalized_of_beam_tracing_beam) and the [vertical normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam], the cylindrical direction cosines obey $k_{R,\mathrm{norm}}^2+k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}}^2+k_{Z,\mathrm{norm}}^2=1$. The [poloidal normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam] is instead a related projection in the meridional plane spanned by $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$.

Sign convention: Positive when the projection of $\mathbf{k}$ onto $\hat{\phi}$ is along the local $+\hat{\phi}$ direction, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
